document_title: What I Need to Know About Eating and Diabetes
text: Target blood glucose for people with diabetes: before meals 70 to 130; 1 to 2 hours after the start of a meal less than 180. Ask your doctor how often to check and for an A1C test at least twice a year.

document_title: What I Need to Know About Eating and Diabetes
text: Low blood glucose (below 70) can make you feel shaky, weak, confused, irritable, hungry, or tired. Have 3-4 glucose tablets, 1/2 cup fruit juice, 1/2 cup regular soft drink, 1 cup milk, 5-6 hard candies, or 1 tablespoon sugar or honey; recheck after 15 minutes and repeat until 70 or higher.

document_title: What I Need to Know About Eating and Diabetes
text: The diabetes food pyramid divides foods by content. Eat more from groups at the bottom (starches, vegetables, fruits) and less from the top (fats and sweets). Foods from starches, fruits, vegetables, and milk groups are highest in carbohydrate and affect blood glucose most.

document_title: What I Need to Know About Eating and Diabetes
section_title: How much should I eat each day?
text: About 1,200 to 1,600 calories a day: 6 starches, 2 milks, 3 vegetables, 4 to 6 ounces meat and meat substitutes, 2 fruits, up to 3 fats. Make a meal plan with your diabetes teacher that fits routine and medicines.

document_title: What I Need to Know About Eating and Diabetes
text: Starches are bread, grains, cereal, pasta, and starchy vegetables like corn and potatoes. They provide carbohydrate, vitamins, minerals, and fiber. Whole grain starches are healthier. Eat some starches at each meal.

document_title: What I Need to Know About Eating and Diabetes
section_title: How much is a serving of starch?
text: One starch serving: 1 slice bread, 1 small potato, 1/2 cup cooked cereal or 3/4 cup dry cereal flakes, or 1 6-inch tortilla. Two servings: 2 slices bread. Three servings: 1 cup rice.

document_title: What I Need to Know About Eating and Diabetes
text: Vegetables provide vitamins, minerals, and fiber. They are low in carbohydrate. Examples: lettuce, broccoli, peppers, carrots, green beans, spinach, tomatoes.

document_title: What I Need to Know About Eating and Diabetes
text: Fruits provide carbohydrate, vitamins, minerals, and fiber. Examples: apples, bananas, oranges, berries, mango, papaya. Choose whole fruit more often than juice; whole fruit is more filling and has more fiber.

document_title: What I Need to Know About Eating and Diabetes
text: Milk provides carbohydrate, protein, calcium, vitamins, and minerals. Drink fat-free (skim) or low-fat (1%) milk. If pregnant or breastfeeding, have four to five servings of milk each day.

document_title: What I Need to Know About Eating and Diabetes
text: The meat group includes meat, poultry, eggs, cheese, fish, and tofu. Eat small amounts each day. Three ounces of cooked lean meat is about the size of a deck of cards. Cook in low-fat ways: broil, grill, roast, steam, microwave.

document_title: What I Need to Know About Eating and Diabetes
text: Limit fats and sweets. Fats have a lot of calories; sweets can be high in carbohydrate and fat. Limiting them helps weight and keeps blood glucose and blood fats under control.

document_title: What I Need to Know About Eating and Diabetes
text: Alcoholic drinks have calories but no nutrients. On an empty stomach they can make blood glucose go too low, and they can raise blood fats. Talk with your doctor about how much to have.

document_title: What I Need to Know About Eating and Diabetes
text: Use measuring cups, spoons, or a food scale to keep servings right. A 3-ounce meat serving is about a palm; 1 cup cooked vegetables, salad, or milk is a fist; 1 teaspoon oil or butter is a fingertip.

document_title: What I Need to Know About Eating and Diabetes
text: Being sick can raise blood glucose. Check it every 4 hours, keep taking diabetes medicines, drink at least one cup of calorie-free liquid each hour while awake. Call your provider if glucose stays above 240 for a day, you have ketones, or you vomit repeatedly.
